## Key messages {.unnumbered}

- **Measure contract delivery, not deviation.** Compare the flown trajectory with a declared reference
  trajectory, keep every offset signed, and report time, lateral and vertical dimensions separately.
- **Declare the reference.** For flights subject to air traffic flow management, the filed plan and the
  regulated plan give different answers. In the European sample, regulated flights are a median 8 minutes
  late against the filed plan, but within 1 minute of the regulated plan. Both views are needed; their
  difference measures how much the agreement changed before execution.
- **Use milestones to compare, continuous measures to explain.** Range-ring crossings, top of climb and
  descent, and FIR crossings form a compact set of contract points that works with sparse data. Along-route
  measures (drift, cross-track, level offset) explain what happened between them.
- **Label what was observed.** Outside a region's surveillance area, the flown trajectory is often
  extrapolated from the plan. Each milestone therefore carries an observation status, and only observed
  values enter the measures.
- **Partner data close the gaps.** Milestone observations at the partner end of international flights,
  in a common format, complete the picture. The contribution from AEROTHAI shows that this works without
  conversion.

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

Trajectory-based operations (TBO) change what an operational performance framework has to observe.
Under TBO, each flight is managed against a trajectory that has been shared among, and agreed by, the
airspace user, the air navigation service providers along the route and the airports. Performance is
then no longer only a question of how efficient or punctual a flight was. It is also a question of
whether the agreed trajectory was delivered, how well its future course could be known in advance,
how often and how late it had to be changed, and what those changes meant operationally.

The current operational performance indicators of the ICAO Global Air Navigation Plan (GANP) were not
designed for this. Punctuality measures the end points of a flight; flight-efficiency indicators compare
the flown trajectory with a geometric reference such as the great-circle distance. Neither compares the
flight with what was agreed for it. ICAO working papers have identified this gap explicitly and called
for TBO-specific, airspace-user-oriented performance measures [@icao2022wp131]. Demonstration
activities, such as the Asia-Pacific TBO Pathfinder project, are developing quantitative benefit
metrics, but no validated common set of measures is yet available [@icao2025apactbo].

This technical note proposes and tests a trajectory-analytic approach to that question. It compares a
**reference trajectory**, standing in for the agreed trajectory, with the **flown trajectory**, and
reports the differences at three levels:

- **Milestones**: time, position and level offsets at operationally defined events, from departure
  through boundary crossings to arrival.
- **Continuous deviation**: lateral, along-track (time) and vertical offsets between the milestones.
- **Simple signatures** that scale to global data: the sequence of flight information regions (FIRs)
  traversed, the time offsets at FIR entries, and the difference in distance flown.

The framing is **trajectory-contract delivery** rather than trajectory deviation. A flight can adhere
closely to an inefficient agreement, and a deviation, such as an authorised shortcut, can improve the
outcome. Adherence and efficiency are therefore measured separately, and every deviation keeps its sign.

The note is written for an international working group. The method is generic: it needs a reference
trajectory with planned times and levels, and an observed trajectory. It is developed and tested on
synthetic trajectories with known answers, and then demonstrated on European data, where both the filed
and the flown trajectories are available for every flight.[^eur-data] The European demonstration is a
development set, not a template: other regions will hold different reference trajectories, and the
method is designed to label which reference was used rather than to assume one.

[^eur-data]: In the European network, the Network Manager stores up to three trajectory versions per
flight: the last filed flight plan (Model 1), the plan updated after an air traffic flow management
(ATFM) regulation (Model 2, regulated flights only), and the flown trajectory updated with surveillance
and other operational data (Model 3). The demonstration in this note uses these versions.

The note is organised as follows. @sec-background summarises what the literature and existing
performance frameworks offer for measuring TBO delivery. @sec-method describes the method.
@sec-synthetic introduces the principles and measures on synthetic cases with known answers, including a
test of an established vertical flight-efficiency indicator. @sec-eur applies them to European city pairs,
where the filed, regulated and flown trajectories are all available. @sec-intl extends the approach to
connections between European hubs and partner airports in other regions, where the observation of the
actual flight depends on the data each region can contribute. @sec-conclusions summarises the findings
and proposes next steps for the PBWG.

## Background: measuring TBO delivery {#sec-background}

### What is being measured

Measuring TBO performance involves at least four distinct objects, which a single trajectory-distance
score cannot capture:

| Object | Question | Example measures |
|---|---|---|
| Agreement delivery | Did the flight satisfy the applicable trajectory and its constraints? | time offset at milestones, tolerance compliance, lateral and vertical offsets |
| Predictability | How accurately could the flight's future passage be known at a given decision time? | prediction error by look-ahead horizon, jumps in estimated times |
| Stability | How much did the agreement change before execution, and how late? | number, size and lead time of revisions |
| Operational consequence | What did the differences cost or save? | fuel, time, resource occupancy |

These objects can conflict. Frequent renegotiation can produce excellent adherence to the latest
agreement while delivering poor predictability against earlier commitments. Monitoring therefore needs
both a **fixed baseline**, frozen at a declared milestone, and the **applicable agreement** in force
when each part of the flight was executed.

### Which trajectory is the reference?

"Planned and agreed" covers several different objects, which answer different questions:

- the **preferred** trajectory of the airspace user;
- the **filed** flight plan, or a system reconstruction of it;
- the **agreed** trajectory, with evidence of acceptance and an effective period;
- a **predicted** trajectory issued by a named system at a recorded time;
- the **executed** trajectory, observed by surveillance.

A filed or predicted trajectory should not be promoted to "agreed" because it is the best available
record. The NASA Management by Trajectory concept, for instance, distinguishes assigned trajectory
constraints from trajectory descriptions, aircraft intent and predictions [@fernandes2018]. An aircraft
can change its intent while remaining within its assigned constraints. Retrospective studies have used
the last filed plan as a proxy for the agreed trajectory, while stating the limitation explicitly
[@prats2019]. This note follows the same practice and labels every result with the reference used.

### How trajectories are aligned

Comparing two trajectories requires a rule for which points correspond. Three rules answer different
questions:

- **Same clock time**: where was the aircraft relative to its agreed position at that instant? This
  combines spatial and timing differences.
- **Same progress along the route**: how did the flown geometry and vertical profile differ,
  independently of timing?
- **Same operational event**: when and how did the aircraft cross a fix, a boundary, the top of
  descent or an arrival constraint?

These views are complementary. Shape-matching methods such as dynamic time warping can help compare
geometry, but they remove precisely the timing offsets that TBO monitoring must expose. Comparative
studies outside aviation also show that rankings of trajectories depend on the chosen similarity
measure [@tao2021]. Generic similarity indices are therefore not used as primary measures here.

### Existing measures and their evidence

@tbl-evidence summarises the methods most directly reusable for TBO delivery, with the level of evidence
behind each. The distinction matters: several indicators frequently cited in TBO discussions were
proposed but never implemented.

| Measure | Source | Evidence level | Use in this note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Timing error at critical points (variance of actual minus planned time) | APACHE project [@apache2018] | proposed, not implemented | time offset at milestones, drift |
| Planned–actual passage-time differences in a TBO framework | @ruiz2018 | simulation | time offset at milestones |
| Signed planned–actual route-length difference; deviation hotspots on route-point pairs | @bongiorno2017 | demonstrated on recorded traffic | distance difference; FIR sequence |
| Track mapping to published routes; progress-based predictability | @andreevamori2024 | demonstrated on recorded traffic | lateral offset, progress mapping |
| Distance-based flight efficiency against filed and actual trajectories | horizontal flight efficiency [@ectrl-hfe] | operational | precedent for distance accounting |
| Flown versus filed flight level with a tolerance band | vertical en-route indicator [@ectrl-vfe-rp4]^[The indicator is used in the European Single Sky performance scheme, reference period 4 (RP4). It is referred to as the RP4 indicator in this note.] | operational | level offset; tested in @sec-synthetic |
| Revisions per flight from tolerance inconsistency; aggregate revision burden | APACHE project [@apache2018] | proposed, not implemented | revision–execution split |
| Tolerance windows at a controlled time of arrival under wind uncertainty | @tan2022 | analytical / model | outlook: tolerance windows |
| Estimated-time-of-arrival error by look-ahead time; jumps and creep in predictions | @enea2013 | demonstrated on recorded traffic | outlook: needs archived predictions |
| Fuel decomposition into planning and execution components | @prats2019; @kuljanin2021 | demonstrated, modelled fuel | outlook: consequence |
| Probabilistic and adaptive conformance monitoring | @zheng2012; @sotiriou2016; @yan2017 | analytical / simulation | outlook |
| Flexibility: remaining feasible options and disturbance tolerance | @idris2008 | analytical | outlook |

: Measures relevant to TBO delivery and the evidence behind them. "Operational" means used in routine
performance monitoring; "proposed" means defined in a report but not implemented. {#tbl-evidence}

Two points stand out. First, the distance-based flight-efficiency indicators are mature, but they
measure efficiency against a geometric reference, not adherence to an agreed trajectory. Differencing
the filed-plan and actual-trajectory versions of such an indicator at aggregate level is not a
measure of plan delivery. Second, the vertical indicator compares flown and filed levels with explicit
tolerances, but counts flying above the plan as satisfactory. It combines an efficiency judgement with
an adherence test. @sec-synthetic examines what this means on cases with a known answer.

### Scope of this note

The method concentrates on agreement delivery, the first of the four objects, with what can be
measured from filed and flown trajectories:

- time offsets at milestones and along the route, separating departure delay from delay gained or
  recovered in the air;
- lateral offsets, route changes and the difference in distance flown;
- level offsets, top-of-climb and top-of-descent shifts, and the distance flown below the requested
  cruise level;
- the sequence of FIRs and the time offsets at FIR entries;
- a minimal view of stability: where a flight was given a revised trajectory before departure, the time
  offset splits exactly into a revision part and an execution part.

Predictability, full revision histories, the sharing of agreements among stakeholders, and operational
consequences require data that are not generally archived today: issued predictions with their issue
times, accepted agreement versions with acceptance times and tolerances, and fuel or cost references.
They are listed as **data requirements** for a future stage rather than addressed here.

Cross-regional comparison also needs a common **measurement specification**: the reference version and
its cut-off time, phase boundaries, surveillance coverage, interpolation rules, altitude datum,
tolerances and aggregation weights. Context such as weather, demand, airspace restrictions, aircraft
capability and flight length must be reported alongside the measures. An observed deviation is not, by
itself, evidence of avoidable inefficiency or of the performance of a particular service provider.

## Method {#sec-method}

### Reference and actual trajectory

Each flight is compared against one **reference trajectory** R, a stand-in for the agreed trajectory.
In the European worked example this is the last filed flight plan (Model 1), or the trajectory after
ATFM regulation (Model 2) if the flight was regulated. The **actual trajectory** A is the flown
trajectory (Model 3). The reference used is recorded with every result. Model 1 and Model 2 are proxies
for an agreed trajectory, not agreements in the TBO sense: neither carries acceptance times or
tolerances.

Where both versions exist, the time offset at any common event splits exactly into a revision part and
an execution part:

$$
\underbrace{t_{M3} - t_{M1}}_{\text{total}} =
\underbrace{(t_{M2} - t_{M1})}_{\text{revision}} +
\underbrace{(t_{M3} - t_{M2})}_{\text{execution}}
$$

For unregulated flights the revision part is zero. Lateral and vertical offsets do not add up in this
way. They are reported separately against each reference.

The method is a **reference-anchored, contract view**: the question is always how far the actual
flight is from what was agreed, not how far the plan is from the flight. Three alignments are kept
apart, because each answers a different question:

| Alignment | Question | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Same position along the reference | When did the flight pass this point of the plan? | time offset $\Delta t(s)$, lateral offset $d(s)$, level offset $\Delta FL(s)$ |
| Same clock time | Where is the flight relative to where it should be now? | distance offset $\Delta s(t)$ |
| Same operational event | When and where did the flight reach a milestone? | milestone offsets in time, position and level |

Shape-only alignments such as dynamic time warping are not used as primary measures, because they
remove the timing offset the comparison is meant to expose.

Sign conventions are fixed throughout: $\Delta t > 0$ means late, $\Delta s > 0$ means ahead of the plan,
$d > 0$ means to the right of the reference track, and $\Delta FL > 0$ means above the reference.

### Densifying both trajectories

Filed plans are sparse: they contain route points and points where the level changes, often tens of
nautical miles apart. Surveillance-based trajectories are dense but irregular, and partner data may be
sparse as well. Both trajectories are therefore densified onto regular grids before they are compared:

- the **reference** at a fixed step along its path (1 NM). This defines the **reference progress** $s$,
  the distance along the reference from its first point. Every position on the plan has a planned time
  $t_R(s)$ and a planned level $FL_R(s)$;
- the **actual trajectory** at a fixed time step (30 s).

Between consecutive points, position is interpolated along the great circle, and time and flight level
linearly.[^projection] Anchoring on the reference has a practical advantage at global scale: a filed plan
almost always exists, whereas the observed trajectory may be sparse.

[^projection]: In the implementation, each flight is projected onto a local plane centred on the route,
and positions are interpolated linearly in that plane. Over the leg lengths of a filed plan the
difference from great-circle interpolation is negligible. The synthetic cases are planar by
construction.

### Projecting the actual trajectory

Each densified actual position is projected onto the reference **segments**, not onto the nearest
reference point, so its progress $s_A$ is continuous. The projection also gives the **signed cross-track
distance** $d$, positive to the right of the reference track.

The projection is **monotone**: each position is searched for only within a window around the progress
already reached (30 NM back, 60 NM ahead). This prevents a point from being matched to a distant part of
the route that happens to pass nearby, for example where a route doubles back. Progress never decreases:
during holdings and vectoring the flight accumulates time without progress, rather than negative distance.
The number of backward steps of the raw projection is kept as a holding signature.

### Deviations on a common grid

Time, level and lateral offset are evaluated on the **common reference grid** $s$. At each reference
step, the time at which the actual flight reached that progress, $t_A(s)$, and its level, $FL_A(s)$, are
interpolated from the densified actual trajectory:

$$
\Delta t(s) = t_A(s) - t_R(s), \qquad
\Delta FL(s) = FL_A(s) - FL_R(s), \qquad
d(s)
$$

Because each reference step carries the same weight, the result does not depend on how densely the
actual flight reported. The same-time view is evaluated on the actual trajectory's time grid:

$$
\Delta s(t) = s_A(t) - s_R(t)
$$

where $s_R(t)$ is the planned progress at clock time $t$. $\Delta s$ is defined only while the
reference flight is itself airborne.

### Validity mask, route changes and coverage

The continuous measures are evaluated only where the projection is meaningful:

- **Terminal exclusion**: each trajectory is cut at its **own** 40 NM ring crossings, i.e. the D40 and
  A40 milestones. The reference grid is restricted to the reference's own D40–A40 span, and the actual
  trajectory to its own D40–A40 times. Inside the rings, departure and arrival procedures and runway
  configuration dominate. The terminal phase is covered by the milestones and by taxi and terminal-area
  measures of the kind documented in TN-01 and TN-02.
- **Route change (off-route span)**: a sustained excursion from the reference route. A span starts and
  ends where $|d|$ crosses 5 NM, must reach $|d| > 20$ NM, and must be at least 10 NM long. The two
  thresholds (hysteresis) make the span cover the whole excursion, not only its outer part. Inside a
  span no point-wise time or level offset is computed, because the flight is not flying the reference
  route. Instead, each span is reported as a whole: its extent along the reference, the **extra
  distance** flown (actual path length minus the reference distance it replaces), and the **time offset
  at re-join**, where the flight is back on the reference.

**Coverage** is the share of the eligible reference grid that is observed. A reference step counts as
observed if the actual flight passed it within 15 NM, along its own path, of a real report, i.e. half
the 30 NM gap threshold. Only the part of a reporting gap that exceeds 30 NM therefore counts as
unobserved: a 35 NM gap loses 5 NM, a 105 NM gap loses 75 NM. Densified points are never counted as
observations. Coverage is reported with every indicator, because an unobserved segment is not a
compliant one.

The 1 NM and 30 s steps, the projection window, the 40 NM terminal radius, the 5/20/10 NM route-change
parameters and the 30 NM gap threshold are working values to be tested on the European data.

### Flight-level summaries

Each flight is summarised by measures that are kept separate rather than combined into an index:

- **Temporal**: time offset at the first and last valid point, and the **drift** between them. Drift
  separates delay inherited from departure from delay gained or recovered in the air.
- **Lateral**: median and maximum $|d|$; number, extent and extra distance of off-route spans, with the
  time offset at re-join; and the signed difference in distance flown (negative means a shorter
  actual path). The distance difference is decomposed by zone:

  $$
  \Delta L = \Delta L_{dep} + \Delta L_{enr} + \Delta L_{arr}
  $$

  where $\Delta L_{dep}$ and $\Delta L_{arr}$ compare the distance flown inside each trajectory's own
  40 NM rings, and $\Delta L_{enr}$ is the en-route remainder, to which the off-route spans contribute.
- **Vertical**: mean $\Delta FL$; the **symmetric share** (grid steps within ±1,000 ft of the reference);
  the **RP4 share** (within or above, as in the European vertical en-route indicator); the distance cruised
  more than 1,000 ft below the requested cruise level; and the TOC/TOD offsets in time and distance.
- **Coverage** as defined above.

Shares are weighted by reference progress, so a holding adds no weight and denser reporting does not
give a flight more weight.

TOC and TOD are where a trajectory first reaches and last leaves its own maximum level less 1,000 ft.
They are interpolated between reports, and computed separately on the reference and the actual
trajectory. The same definition is used for the synthetic cases and for the operational data.

### Milestone engine

The milestones are computed **independently on each trajectory** and then joined by name, so the
comparison is symmetric and needs no point matching:

| Milestone | Definition |
|---|---|
| DEP, ARR | First and last point (in real data: AOBT/ATOT and ALDT/AIBT from APDF where available) |
| D40, D100, D200 | First exit from the circle of that radius around the departure airport |
| A200, A100, A40 | Last entry into the circle of that radius around the arrival airport |
| FIR entries | Every change of FIR, numbered by occurrence (re-entering a FIR is a new event). In the European data, the upper and lower parts of a FIR (FIR/UIR) are merged and visits shorter than 60 s are discarded; for the comparison of FIR sequences each FIR is counted once, at its first entry |
| TOC, TOD | As defined above |

Crossing times and positions are located on the line between two reports by bisection, not snapped to
the nearest report. In the output, every milestone is tagged as present on both trajectories, only on the
reference, or only on the actual flight. A milestone present on one side only, such as an additional FIR,
is itself a result. For common milestones the time, position and level offsets are reported, together
with the **segment-wise change** in time offset from the previous common milestone. These changes add
up to the arrival offset minus the departure offset, the same accounting as the delay chain in TN-02.

The **FIR sequence** is reported as a whole and compared between the two trajectories. With the FIR
entry time offsets, it is the cheapest signature of plan delivery and works with coarse partner data.

### Tolerance windows

Under TBO, an agreement carries tolerances: a time window at a constraint point, a lateral corridor, a
vertical band. Delivery is then measured as compliance with the window and, if outside, by how much:

$$
\text{early exceedance} = \max(L - t_A,\, 0), \qquad
\text{late exceedance} = \max(t_A - U,\, 0)
$$

for a window $[L, U]$ at a constraint point. Early and late exceedances are reported separately, because
they have different operational consequences, and windows may be asymmetric.

Agreed TBO tolerances are not yet recorded in operational data. The nearest existing case is the
**take-off window of an ATFM slot**: a regulated flight is expected to take off within a stated window
around its calculated take-off time (CTOT).[^ctot] This window is used as a **proxy tolerance**, and
labelled as such. It differs from a TBO tolerance in three respects: it is imposed by flow management
rather than agreed, it applies at a single point (take-off) rather than along the trajectory, and it
exists only for regulated flights. Its value for this note is methodological: it allows the
compliance and exceedance measures to be specified and tested on real data before agreed windows exist.
Where partners operate ATFM programmes with their own slot or departure-time windows, the same
specification applies with their window definitions.

[^ctot]: In the European network, ATFM slot adherence uses a window of −5 to +10 minutes around the CTOT.
Other ATFM systems define their own windows.

Tolerance windows derived from the data themselves, such as the range of routinely flown behaviour, are
not used as agreement tolerances. An empirical envelope describes what usually happens; it does not say
what was agreed.

### Aggregation

Flight-level results are aggregated according to the question asked, and the rule is stated with every
aggregate:

- **Flight scorecards** give each flight equal weight: the share of flights within a band, the
  distribution of drift or of the time offset at a milestone.
- **Exposure views** sum numerators and denominators over flights: total distance flown off-route over
  total eligible distance, total time outside a window over total time. These describe the traffic
  rather than the typical flight, and long flights weigh more.
- **Percentiles** are computed on the pooled flight-level values of the declared unit (flight, or
  flight segment). Percentiles of sub-groups are never averaged to obtain an overall percentile.
- **Signed values, absolute size and compliance are kept separate.** A mean signed offset close to zero
  can hide early and late flights that cancel out; a standard deviation can hide a uniformly late
  operation; a compliance share hides the size of the exceedances. Bias, spread and tail are therefore
  reported together, for example the mean, the mean absolute value and the 90th percentile of the
  absolute value.
- **Coverage** is reported with every aggregate, as the share of eligible distance, or of eligible
  flights, that could be assessed.

Uncertainty intervals for aggregates are computed by resampling whole operating days or traffic flows,
not individual trajectory points, which are strongly dependent.

## Synthetic test cases {#sec-synthetic}

Before the method is applied to European flight data, it is checked on synthetic trajectories whose
deviations are known by construction. Each case isolates one phenomenon: a pure clock shift, a lateral
offset, a level change, a detour or a surveillance gap. For each case, the expected value of every
measure was stated before the calculation. The cases serve three purposes:

- **Verification**: the algorithm measures what it is meant to measure, and nothing else.
- **Justification of design choices**: for example, anchoring on the reference trajectory, or keeping
  time and space offsets as separate measures.
- **Reference cases for discussion**: they make the behaviour of an indicator visible on trajectories
  whose ground truth is beyond doubt, which is used below to discuss the vertical en-route indicator.

The synthetic geometry is planar and expressed in nautical miles. The reference flight covers 600 NM
at 7 NM/min with a cruise level of FL350. The reference is supplied as sparse plan points, as filed
flight plans are, and the actual flight as 30-second surveillance-like reports. Measures are evaluated
outside 40 NM of either airport; inside that radius the terminal (ASMA) milestones apply.

### Case catalogue and verification

@tbl-cases lists the cases and their outcomes. All checks pass.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cases
#| tbl-cap: "Synthetic cases: expected behaviour and outcome of the automated check."
bind_rows(check_cases(res), check_mst(mst)) |>
  mutate(pass = if_else(pass, "pass", "FAIL")) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(case = "Case", expectation = "Expected behaviour", pass = "Check")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Selected measures per synthetic case. Time offsets in minutes (+ = late), distances in NM,
#|   levels in FL. Shares are distance-weighted along the reference."
summ |>
  select(case, dt_entry, drift, ds_med, d_max_abs, dfl_mean, share_sym, share_rp4,
         ddist_nm, coverage) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(-case, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(case = "Case", dt_entry = "Δt entry", drift = "Drift", ds_med = "Δs (median)",
             d_max_abs = "max |d|", dfl_mean = "ΔFL mean", share_sym = "Symmetric share",
             share_rp4 = "RP4 share", ddist_nm = "Δ distance", coverage = "Coverage")
```

### Same position or same time? (C02/C13)

A flight that departs 10 minutes late but otherwise flies its plan exactly is the simplest possible
deviation. @fig-space-time shows it in two ways. Compared at the same position along the reference,
the flight is 10 minutes late throughout. Compared at the same clock time, it is 70 NM behind its
planned position. Both describe one fact. The time view answers "when did the flight pass this
point?", which is what milestone- and gate-based monitoring requires. The position view answers "where
should the aircraft be now?", which is the 4D view of a controller or a ground system.

The method therefore reports both. The time view is the primary one, because it does not depend on
ground speed: 10 minutes of delay is 70 NM at cruise speed but considerably less in the terminal area.
Shape-only alignments such as dynamic time warping would remove the offset entirely and are not used
as primary measures.

```{r}
#| label: fig-space-time
#| fig-cap: "C13: a departure delay of 10 minutes seen at the same position (time offset) and at the same
#|   clock time (distance offset). Gaps at the start and end: the measures are evaluated only outside
#|   the 40 NM terminal radius and while both flights are airborne."
#| fig-height: 5
plot_space_time(res)
```

### Departure delay versus delay gained in the air (C02/C03, C15)

With the reference as anchor, the time offset is known continuously along the route. Its change between
two points, the *drift*, separates delay inherited from departure from delay accumulated or recovered
in the air. In C02 (clock shift) the offset is +10 minutes at entry and the drift is zero. In C03, a 5%
speed reduction after 150 NM, the offset starts at zero and builds up to
`r sprintf("%.2f", summ$drift[summ$case == "C03 airborne slowdown"])` minutes.

The same idea at milestone level gives the segment-wise change in time offset, used in TN-02 for the
turnaround chain. @fig-chain shows C15: a flight leaves 8 minutes late, recovers 1.8 minutes en route,
and loses 2.4 minutes in descent. The segment changes add up exactly to the arrival offset minus the
departure offset, so every minute is accounted for at a named point of the flight.

```{r}
#| label: fig-chain
#| fig-cap: "C15: time offset at common milestones (D/A rings, FIR entries, TOC/TOD). Departure delay
#|   8 min, partial recovery en route, loss in descent."
plot_milestone_chain(mst)
```

### Route changes and FIR sequences (C14)

At global scale, a dense trajectory comparison is not always possible. A cheaper signature is the
sequence of FIRs traversed and the time offset at each FIR entry. In C14 the flight detours north
around an area and briefly enters FIR D (@fig-fir). The FIR sequence changes from A–B–C to
A–B–D–B–C. The milestone engine records the two additional entries as present only in the actual
trajectory, and every common milestone after the detour is 4.0 minutes late. FIR entries are numbered
by occurrence, so re-entering a FIR is a separate event rather than overwriting the first entry.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fir
#| fig-cap: "C14: detour through FIR D. Points mark FIR entries; the entries into D and the second
#|   entry into B exist only in the actual trajectory."
#| fig-height: 3.2
plot_fir_detour(mst)
```

### What the vertical en-route indicator measures (C09, C16)

The European RP4 vertical en-route indicator compares flown and filed levels and counts distance
flown within ±1,000 ft of the plan *or above it* as satisfactory. It is referenced here as an
established European indicator. The synthetic cases show which question it answers and which it does
not (@fig-vertical).

- **C09**: the flight cruises at FL390 against a filed FL350. The RP4 share is 1.00. A symmetric share
  that counts only distance within ±1,000 ft of the plan is 0.32. The indicator judges vertical
  efficiency (higher is generally better), not adherence to the plan.
- **C16**: the filed plan is already capped at FL310, whereas the requested cruise level was FL350. The
  flight follows the plan exactly; both shares are 1.00. About
  `r round(summ$cruise_below_rfl_nm[summ$case == "C16 capped reference"])` NM are flown 4,000 ft below
  the requested level, which no indicator measured against the filed plan can detect.

Taken together, the two cases show that the indicator mixes two questions: whether the plan was
delivered, and whether the vertical profile was efficient. It answers neither completely. The proposed
method therefore reports the signed level offset, a symmetric adherence share, and the distance flown
below the requested level as separate measures. Whether the cases occur at a relevant scale is
examined on the European data (@sec-rp4-tests).

```{r}
#| label: fig-vertical
#| fig-cap: "C09 and C16: vertical profiles against the reference with the ±1,000 ft band. Dashed line
#|   in C16: requested cruise level (FL350)."
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot_vertical(res)
```

### Limits of the synthetic cases

The cases verify the computation, not the operational meaning of the measures. Three behaviours need
attention when the method moves to real data:

- **Sparse tracks**: on the common reference grid, the drift is reproduced exactly with 2-minute and
  5-minute reports, and coverage degrades gradually (1.00 and 0.90). An earlier rule, which counted a
  whole gap as unobserved once it exceeded the threshold, collapsed coverage to near zero at 5-minute
  reporting although the timing result was correct; it was replaced by the excess-gap rule. The
  vertical measures are less robust. Linear interpolation between sparse reports cuts the corners of
  climb and descent: with 5-minute reports the top of descent appears 6 NM early and the symmetric
  share drops to 0.93, although the flight followed the plan exactly. For sparse partner data, vertical
  measures should therefore be reported with the reporting interval, and TOC/TOD offsets smaller than
  about one reporting interval should not be interpreted.
- **Planar geometry**: real trajectories are projected onto a local plane per flight before the method
  is applied.
- **Level offsets on lateral offsets**: a parallel offset makes the actual path slightly longer, which
  produces a small apparent level offset in climb and descent (C04:
  `r sprintf("%+.2f", summ$dfl_mean[summ$case == "C04 parallel offset 5 NM"])` FL on average).

## Testing the vertical indicator on operational data {#sec-rp4-tests}

The synthetic cases show *how* the RP4 vertical indicator can mislead; they do not show *how often*
it does. Before a group of regions considers adopting a vertical indicator of this kind, five hypotheses
should be tested on operational data. Two are demonstrated synthetically above. @tbl-rp4-hyp lists all
five, and @tbl-vertical gives first results from the European sample of @sec-eur (950 flights).

| | Hypothesis | Synthetic evidence | Test on operational data |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | Counting flight above the plan as satisfactory mixes efficiency with adherence | C09 | Indicator next to the symmetric share and the signed level offset; share of flights where the two disagree, and whether rankings of airports, flows or regions change |
| H2 | Restrictions already in the plan are invisible | C16 | Filed versus requested cruise level; share of flights scoring "within" while cruising below the requested level |
| H3 | The indicator is blind to revisions | — | Indicator against the last filed plan and against the revised plan (Model 1, Model 2); revision and execution parts of the level offset for regulated flights |
| H4 | The indicator ignores time | — | TOC and TOD offsets in time and distance, and level-off duration in climb and descent, for flights with the same indicator value |
| H5 | Results depend on the tolerance band and the weighting | — | Band of ±500, ±1,000 and ±2,000 ft; distance-weighted versus flight-weighted; per flow versus pooled |

: Hypotheses for evaluating the RP4 vertical indicator. {#tbl-rp4-hyp}

```{r tbl-vertical}
#| label: tbl-vertical
#| tbl-cap: "Vertical measures against the filed plan, European sample, 1–14 June 2025 (medians over
#|   flights). Shares are weighted by distance along the reference, en route only."
#| eval: !expr has_ops
tab_vertical(cf) |> rename(`Airport pair` = PAIR) |> gt_tn() |>
  fmt_number(c(`Within ±1,000 ft`, `Within or above`), decimals = 2)
```

The first results support H1 and qualify H2 to H4:

- **H1 – confirmed in the sample.** The two shares differ by more than 0.10 for a large share of
  flights, up to about 90% on London–Munich, where flights often cruise above the filed level. The
  "within or above" share is therefore mainly a statement about efficiency on these flows.
- **H2 – not visible in the filed plans.** In this sample the filed cruise level never lies below the
  requested level, so restrictions do not enter the plan in the way C16 assumes. The distance cruised
  below the requested level comes from the flown profile (median 9–38 NM per pair), mainly on short
  flights, and is not captured by either share.
- **H3 – small effect here.** For regulated flights, the shares change by more than 0.05 between the
  filed and the regulated plan for fewer than 1% of flights: the regulations in the sample shifted times
  and, rarely, routes, but almost never levels.
- **H4 – confirmed.** Among flights with a "within or above" share of at least 0.85, the top-of-descent
  offset still ranges from about −3 to +23 minutes (10th to 90th percentile). The share says nothing about
  when the descent took place.
- **H5 – partly confirmed.** The symmetric share and the ranking of flows depend on the band width; the weighting matters only across flows of different length (see below).

**H3 – revisions.** The indicator compares the flight with the last filed plan. Where a revised
trajectory changes the planned level, a flight that follows its revision exactly can score poorly, and
a flight that ignores it can score well. For regulated flights, the level offset is split in the same
way as the time offset: the difference between the revised and the filed plan (revision), and between
the flight and the revised plan (execution). Because level offsets are not additive along a
trajectory, the split is reported at common points of progress rather than as a single number.

**H4 – time.** A share of distance within a band says nothing about when the flight reached its
level or how long it took. Two flights with the same indicator value can differ by several minutes in
top of climb, top of descent or time spent levelled off in climb. The test compares these quantities
across flights grouped by indicator value; a wide spread within a group shows that the indicator does
not capture them.

**H5 – sensitivity.** The ±1,000 ft band, distance weighting and pooling are conventions. The test
recomputes the indicator under alternative conventions and checks whether conclusions change,
in particular rankings between flows, airports or regions. An indicator whose ranking depends on the
band width or on the weighting is unsuitable for comparison across regions with different traffic
mixes and flight lengths.

@tbl-h5 shows both shares for the six European flows with bands of ±500, ±1,000 and ±2,000 ft.

```{r tbl-h5}
#| label: tbl-h5
#| tbl-cap: "H5: vertical shares against the filed plan for three band widths, distance-weighted, en route,
#|   European sample (950 flights)."
#| eval: !expr has_ops
tab_h5(h5_load()) |> gt_tn(groupname_col = "Share") |> fmt_number(where(is.double), decimals = 2)
```

The results answer H5 in two parts:

- **Weighting.** Within a flow, flight-weighted and distance-weighted shares differ by at most 0.03,
  because the flights of a flow have similar lengths. The weighting matters only when flows of different
  length are pooled, which is the cross-regional case. It cannot be tested within this sample and
  remains a requirement for the measurement specification.
- **Band width.** The symmetric share depends strongly on the band: it rises by 0.10 to 0.20 between
  ±500 and ±2,000 ft, and the ranking of the flows changes. London–Munich is always last, but Munich–London
  moves from third place with the narrow band to first place with the wide band. The "within or above"
  share is less sensitive, because it already accepts all flight above the plan, and its ranking is
  stable except for one swap between neighbouring flows.

A vertical adherence share is therefore only comparable between regions if the band is part of the
specification and reported with the result.

**Global relevance.** The hypotheses matter most for comparison across regions. Three conditions vary
between regions and interact with the indicator's design:

- **What the reference contains.** In some systems the filed plan already includes level restrictions
  and capping; in others the filed level is the airspace user's request. The same flown profile then
  scores differently (H2).
- **How often plans are revised, and whether revisions are recorded.** Regions with frequent or
  unrecorded revisions are compared against an outdated reference (H3).
- **Traffic mix and flight length.** Distance weighting gives long-haul flights more weight; regions
  with different mixes are not comparable without stating the weighting (H5).

The outcome is reported neutrally. If the hypotheses are not confirmed at a relevant scale, the
indicator is a reasonable summary of vertical adherence in practice. If they are confirmed, the note
recommends reporting the components separately: the signed level offset, a symmetric adherence share,
the distance flown below the requested level, and the TOC/TOD offsets. In either case, the requirement
for a global indicator is the same: the reference used, and what it contains, must be declared.

## European city pairs: measuring contract delivery {#sec-eur}

```{r eur-guard}
#| include: false
# The operational chapters need the local data products in data/tbo/ (not distributed).
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_ops)
```

This chapter applies the principles of @sec-synthetic to real flights. It uses the European network
because, for each flight, three trajectory versions are archived by the Network Manager: the last filed
plan (Model 1, M1), the plan re-issued after an ATFM regulation (Model 2, M2, regulated flights only)
and the flown trajectory (Model 3, M3). This makes it possible to measure delivery against two
different references for the same flight, and so to test the questions raised in @sec-background:
which reference, which alignment, and what the difference means.

### Sample and data

Six directions between six PBWG study airports were selected for 1–14 June 2025
(@tbl-eur-sample). They cover a short connection with dense airspace structure (London–Munich), a
medium-haul connection across several FIRs (Amsterdam–Madrid), and a longer connection to the
south-east of the network (Frankfurt–Istanbul). The pairs are illustrative, not representative of the
network.

```{r tbl-eur-sample}
#| label: tbl-eur-sample
#| tbl-cap: "European sample, 1–14 June 2025. Regulated = flight has a Model 2 trajectory."
tab_sample(d) |> rename(`Airport pair` = PAIR) |> gt_tn()
```

For every flight the milestone table of TN-01 is built for each trajectory version: range-ring
crossings at 40, 100 and 200 NM around both aerodromes, top of climb and top of descent, and FIR
crossings. The actual trajectory is then compared with each available reference in a common milestone
table (one row per flight, milestone and reference; @sec-annex-data).

### Which reference? Filed versus regulated plan

About two thirds of the flights in the sample were regulated. For them, the filed plan is no longer the
trajectory the flight was expected to fly: the regulation moved the take-off time and, in some cases,
the route. @tbl-eur-refs shows the time offset at the first and last range ring against both references.

```{r tbl-eur-refs}
#| label: tbl-eur-refs
#| tbl-cap: "Regulated flights: time offset actual − reference at 40 NM after departure (D40) and before
#|   arrival (A40), median and interquartile range (IQR), in minutes. M1 = filed plan, M2 = regulated plan."
tab_pair_refs(d) |>
  gt_tn(groupname_col = "PAIR") |>
  cols_label(MST = "Milestone", med_M1 = "Median", iqr_M1 = "IQR", med_M2 = "Median", iqr_M2 = "IQR") |>
  tab_spanner("against M1 (filed)", c(med_M1, iqr_M1)) |>
  tab_spanner("against M2 (regulated)", c(med_M2, iqr_M2))
```

Against the filed plan, regulated flights appear between 4 and 11 minutes late at every milestone, with
a wide spread. Against the regulated plan, the median offset falls to within about three minutes for most
pairs (six minutes at most, for arrivals in Istanbul) and
the spread roughly halves. The choice of reference therefore changes the reading of the same flight from
"late" to "on time". Both readings are correct: the first measures delivery of the original
commitment, the second delivery of the trajectory in force at departure.

### Revision and execution

Because times at common milestones are additive, the total offset against the filed plan splits exactly
into a **revision** part (regulated minus filed plan) and an **execution** part (flown minus regulated
plan), as introduced in @sec-method. @tbl-eur-decomp shows the split for all regulated flights.

```{r tbl-eur-decomp}
#| label: tbl-eur-decomp
#| tbl-cap: "Revision and execution parts of the time offset at the range rings (median, minutes).
#|   Total = Revision + Execution for each flight."
tab_decomp(d) |>
  gt_tn(groupname_col = "GROUP") |>
  cols_label(MST = "Milestone")
```

For flights with an ATFM delay, the revision accounts for almost all of the offset against the filed plan
(about 11 minutes). Against the regulated plan the flights depart about a minute early and gain
another minute en route. Flights that were regulated without delay show no revision; they leave about
three minutes late and recover most of it before arrival. The execution spread is similar in both
groups (IQR 7–8 minutes).

This is the agreement-stability dimension of @sec-background in its simplest form. A monitoring scheme
that looks only at the latest agreement would report these flights as well delivered; one that looks
only at the filed plan would attribute the regulation delay to the flight. Reporting both parts keeps
the two stories apart.

**Example: DLH1304, Frankfurt–Istanbul, 1 June 2025.** The flight received a 32-minute ATFM delay.
Against the filed plan it is 27 minutes late at D40 and 24 minutes late at A40. Against the regulated
plan it departs 6 minutes early and arrives 8.5 minutes early (@fig-eur-chain). The flight more than
recovered against the trajectory it was given, while still arriving well behind the original plan.

```{r fig-eur-chain}
#| label: fig-eur-chain
#| fig-cap: "DLH1304 EDDF–LTFM, 1 June 2025: time offset of the flown trajectory against the filed and the
#|   regulated plan at range rings and FIR crossings."
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot_chain(d, 285787181)
```

### Reroutes: when the agreement changes the path

A regulation can also change the route. Within the six pairs, the regulated plan departs by more than
5 NM laterally from the filed plan en route for 14 of 611 regulated flights, almost all of them on
Amsterdam–Madrid (@tbl-eur-route).

```{r tbl-eur-route}
#| label: tbl-eur-route
#| tbl-cap: "Regulated flights: route of the regulated plan (M2) compared with the filed plan (M1)."
tab_route_check(d) |> gt_tn(groupname_col = NULL) |> cols_label(GROUP = "")
```

To study reroutes beyond the six pairs, all regulated flights at the ten TN-02 study airports in the same
period were scanned for differences between the filed and regulated routes. Of about 64,000 regulated
flights, about 2,000 (3%) have a different route description and waypoint sequence. A stratified sample
of 100 of them, covering all ten airports and the full range of route-length changes, was examined in
detail. Only 44 differ by more than 5 NM en route; in the others the change is confined to the
departure or arrival procedure. A route-description change is therefore not by itself a reroute. This
note defines a **reroute** as a lateral difference of more than 5 NM between the regulated and filed
plans, excluding the first and last 40 NM.

```{r tbl-eur-reroute}
#| label: tbl-eur-reroute
#| tbl-cap: "Reroute sample (study airports, 1–14 June 2025): en-route lateral and time offset of the flown
#|   trajectory against the filed (M1) and regulated (M2) plan. Medians over flights."
tab_reroute_delivery(d) |> gt_tn(groupname_col = "GROUP") |> cols_label(REF = "Reference")
```

For rerouted flights, the regulated plan is also the better lateral reference: the mean cross-track
distance falls from 3.8 to 2.9 NM and the 95th percentile from 15 to 12 NM (@tbl-eur-reroute). What
remains is the tactical layer, mainly direct routings that neither plan contains. @fig-eur-reroute shows
three typical cases. AFR4147 (Hamburg–Paris) and DLH3RJ (Athens–Frankfurt) follow neither the filed nor
the regulated route for long stretches, taking directs instead; THY1918 (Geneva–Istanbul) follows the
regulated route closely, including the changed arrival.

```{r fig-eur-reroute}
#| label: fig-eur-reroute
#| fig-cap: "Three rerouted flights: filed (M1), regulated (M2) and flown (M3) trajectories."
#| fig-height: 4
lab <- d$rr_keys |> mutate(L = paste(AIRCRAFT_ID, paste(ADEP, ADES, sep = "–"))) |> select(ID, L)
lab_fun <- as_labeller(setNames(lab$L, lab$ID))
plot_map3(d$rr_prof, c(285745366, 286241176, 285903572), labeller = lab_fun)
```

The observation matters for contract delivery: a flight can deviate from its agreement in a way that
shortens it. The lateral offset should therefore be reported with its sign and together with the
difference in distance flown, so that an authorised shortcut is not read as non-compliance.


### Lateral delivery and the FIR sequence

The sequence of FIRs traversed is the simplest lateral signature that also works with sparse data from
other regions (@sec-synthetic, case C14). Counting each FIR once at its first entry, the flown sequence
matches the planned one for almost all flights between Amsterdam and Madrid, but for only about half of
the flights between London and Munich (@tbl-eur-fir).

```{r tbl-eur-fir}
#| label: tbl-eur-fir
#| tbl-cap: "Share of flights whose sequence of FIR crossings matches the filed plan (M1)."
tab_fir_seq(d) |> rename(`Airport pair` = PAIR) |> gt_tn()
```

On London–Munich the route runs close to several FIR boundaries, so a few nautical miles of direct
routing change the FIRs crossed. A FIR-sequence mismatch therefore signals a lateral deviation, not its
size; it should be read together with the cross-track measure.

For regulated flights, the FIR crossings can also be compared with the regulated plan
(@tbl-eur-fir-refs). The share of flights with exactly the planned sequence is almost the same against
both references, because regulations rarely changed the route. The time offset at the FIR entries,
however, drops from a median of about 8 minutes against the filed plan to under 1 minute against the
regulated plan, consistent with the range rings. FIR entries therefore work as contract points in the
same way as the rings, and can carry the revision–execution split.

```{r tbl-eur-fir-refs}
#| label: tbl-eur-fir-refs
#| tbl-cap: "Regulated flights (611): FIR crossings compared with the filed and the regulated plan."
tab_fir_refs(d) |> gt_tn()
```

**Example: AEA36MB, Madrid–Amsterdam, 12 June 2025.** The flight flew 24 NM more than filed. The extra
distance came from radar vectoring in the last 40 NM before Amsterdam (up to 21 NM cross-track), partly
offset by a shortcut en route. In time, it was 9 minutes behind the filed plan at the 40 NM ring after
departure, carried this through the cruise and
arrived about 7 minutes late against the filed plan. Against its regulated plan (10 minutes ATFM delay)
it was 1 minute early at D40 and 3 minutes early at A40. Both the lateral and the temporal pictures are
needed to describe what happened.

### Along the route: drift, lateral and vertical offsets {#sec-eur-cont}

The milestones are complemented by the continuous measures of @sec-method, computed on the reference
grid between the 40 NM rings. @fig-eur-profile shows them for AEA36MB against both references. The
lateral and vertical offsets are the same for both references, because the regulation changed only the
time of this flight. The time offset is shifted by the regulation, but its shape is the same: the flight
lost about 2.5 minutes over the en-route phase against either reference.

```{r fig-eur-profile}
#| label: fig-eur-profile
#| fig-cap: "AEA36MB LEMD–EHAM, 12 June 2025: cross-track distance, level offset and time offset along the
#|   reference, en-route phase (between the 40 NM rings), against the filed and the regulated plan."
#| fig-height: 6
plot_profile_flight(pf_aea)
```

@tbl-eur-measures summarises the proposed flight-level measures for all regulated flights against both
references. Three observations stand out:

- Only the **time offset at entry** depends on the reference. The **drift** en route (median −1.4
  minutes: most flights recover some time in cruise) and all lateral and vertical measures are the same
  against both plans, because regulations in this sample rarely changed the route or the level.
- The **distance difference** is close to zero in the median but has a wide spread. Its split by zone
  shows the pattern seen for AEA36MB: shorter routes en route (directs, median −2.4 NM) and longer paths
  in the last 40 NM before landing (vectoring, up to 19 NM at the 75th percentile).
- **Coverage** of the en-route grid by observed reports is about 0.8. The remainder lies in gaps between
  reports, mostly on long straight segments, where the interpolated values are reliable but are not
  counted as observations.

```{r tbl-eur-measures}
#| label: tbl-eur-measures
#| tbl-cap: "Proposed flight-level measures for regulated flights (611), against the filed (M1) and the
#|   regulated (M2) plan. Median [25th; 75th percentile]. En-route phase between the 40 NM rings unless
#|   stated otherwise."
tab_measures_demo(cf) |> gt() |>
  cols_label(M1 = "against filed plan (M1)", M2 = "against regulated plan (M2)") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(12))
```

@tbl-eur-drift gives the drift per airport pair against the filed plan. On Madrid–Amsterdam flights
recover about 3 minutes en route; on Istanbul–Frankfurt they lose time slightly. The spread is wide for
all pairs: the drift distinguishes delay inherited from departure from delay gained or recovered in the
air for each flight.

```{r tbl-eur-drift}
#| label: tbl-eur-drift
#| tbl-cap: "Time offset at entry and exit of the en-route phase and drift between them, against the filed
#|   plan, all flights (medians; P10 and P90 of the drift). Coverage = share of the en-route grid observed."
tab_drift_pair(cf) |> rename(`Airport pair` = PAIR) |> gt_tn() |> fmt_number(Coverage, decimals = 2)
```

### Tolerance windows: the ATFM slot as a proxy {#sec-eur-window}

@sec-method proposed measuring delivery against a time window, with early and late exceedance reported
separately. No agreed TBO windows exist in the data, but regulated flights have a take-off window around
their calculated take-off time (in the European network, −5 to +10 minutes). @tbl-eur-window applies the
window measures to it.

```{r tbl-eur-window}
#| label: tbl-eur-window
#| tbl-cap: "Regulated flights: take-off within the ATFM slot window (−5 / +10 minutes), with early and late
#|   exceedance. Take-off time derived from off-block time plus taxi time."
tab_slot_window(cf) |> rename(`Airport pair` = PAIR) |> gt_tn()
```

Between 83% and 97% of regulated flights took off within the window. Departures outside it were mostly
early, by less than a minute on average, while the few late departures exceeded the window by several
minutes. A compliance share alone would hide this asymmetry; the exceedances show it. The same
measures apply unchanged to any agreed time window, for example at a metering fix or an arrival
constraint, once such windows are recorded.

### What the European examples show

- The **reference** determines the result. For regulated flights, delivery against the regulated plan
  is tight (median within about ±3 minutes) while the offset against the filed plan is dominated by the
  regulation.
- The **revision–execution split** separates what the network changed from what the flight did, and
  makes agreement stability measurable with data that already exist.
- **Reroutes** are rare (about 3% of regulated flights by route description, fewer by lateral change)
  but visible; the regulated plan is the better lateral reference for them.
- The **tactical layer** (directs, vectoring) remains in all cases. It is part of execution and can be
  beneficial; it should be reported with its sign, not as an error.

## International connections {#sec-intl}

The PBWG's interest is global. This chapter applies the same approach to flights between the European
study airports and seven partner airports in other regions: Toronto (CYYZ), Atlanta (KATL), São Paulo
(SBGR), Tokyo Narita (RJAA), Bangkok (VTBS), Singapore (WSSS) and Beijing (ZBAA), 1–7 June 2025.

### The reference is global, the observation is regional

The filed plan (M1) covers the whole flight, so every milestone can be defined at both ends. The flown
trajectory (M3), however, is built from surveillance and flight data available to the European Network
Manager. Outside that area it is the filed plan shifted in time. At the partner end of the flight it
therefore reproduces the reference rather than observing the flight: in this sample, 92–97% of the range
ring crossings at the partner airport for flights leaving Europe are identical in position and level to
the filed plan.

To avoid reading these points as perfect delivery, every actual milestone carries an **observation
status**: observed, extrapolated, proxy or missing. Extrapolated points are reported as "not observed"
and do not enter the delivery measures.

### Contributing observations at the partner end

Where the European record is extrapolated, other sources can contribute observations of the ring
crossings. They are used in a fixed order: partner data, OpenSky Network ring crossings, and the European
correlated surveillance position profile (CPF) where its points lie on both sides of the ring within five
minutes. @tbl-intl-sources shows the share of 100 NM ring crossings at the partner airport filled by
each source.

```{r tbl-intl-sources}
#| label: tbl-intl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Source of the observed 100 NM ring crossing at the partner airport (A100 = arrival from Europe,
#|   D100 = departure to Europe), share of flights, 1–7 June 2025. No partner data were used in this
#|   demonstration."
tab_intl_sources(d) |> select(INTL, MST, OpenSky, `NM surveillance (CPF)`, `NM flown (M3)`, `not observed`) |>
  gt_tn(groupname_col = NULL) |> fmt_percent(where(is.double), decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(INTL = "Partner airport", MST = "Ring")
```

Coverage differs strongly between partner airports. Observations exist for nearly all flights at
Toronto, Atlanta and Singapore, and for most at Tokyo, while arrivals at São Paulo and Beijing are almost
entirely unobserved from European sources. These gaps are where partner contributions add most: a
partner's own record of the ring crossings, landing and in-block times would turn "not observed" into
"delivered" without any change to the method.

### Delivery at both ends of the flight

@tbl-intl-delivery compares the time offset against the filed plan at the European end and at the
partner end of the flight, using observed milestones only.

```{r tbl-intl-delivery}
#| label: tbl-intl-delivery
#| tbl-cap: "Time offset actual − filed plan (median, minutes) at the European and the partner end of the
#|   flight, observed ring milestones only, 1–7 June 2025."
tab_intl_delivery(d) |>
  select(INTL, DIR, `dt_European end`, `dt_partner end`, `iqr_European end`, `iqr_partner end`) |>
  gt_tn(groupname_col = "INTL") |>
  cols_label(DIR = "Direction", `dt_European end` = "European end", `dt_partner end` = "Partner end",
             `iqr_European end` = "European end", `iqr_partner end` = "Partner end") |>
  tab_spanner("Median", c(`dt_European end`, `dt_partner end`)) |>
  tab_spanner("IQR", c(`iqr_European end`, `iqr_partner end`))
```

The difference between the two ends measures what happened on the long-haul segment outside the European
area: time recovered or lost en route. Without observations at the partner end, this segment is
invisible, and the time offset at arrival simply repeats the offset at departure.

**Example: THA911, London–Bangkok.** The flight left London 32 minutes behind its filed plan. The
European record extrapolates the arrival in Bangkok with the same offset. OpenSky observations of the
100 NM and 40 NM ring crossings around Bangkok show the actual offset at arrival (31 and 33 minutes). In
this case the delay was carried through the flight; the observation confirms it rather than assuming it.

### FIR crossings outside Europe

For the international flights, about 70% of the FIR crossings outside the European area are
extrapolated in the European record (@tbl-intl-fir). The range rings around the partner airport serve as
a first, data-light substitute for these boundaries. Observed FIR crossings in the partner region would
allow the same milestone measures along the whole route.

```{r tbl-intl-fir}
#| label: tbl-intl-fir
#| tbl-cap: "FIR crossings of the international flights by status. INTL = crossing into a FIR outside the
#|   European area; ENR = crossings within it."
tab_intl_fir_obs(d) |> gt_tn(groupname_col = NULL) |> cols_label(SIDE = "")
```

### A partner contribution: milestones from AEROTHAI {#sec-tha}

```{r tha-load}
#| include: false
has_tha <- tha_has_data()
if (has_tha) th <- tha_load()
```

During the preparation of this note, AEROTHAI (Aeronautical Radio of Thailand), the air navigation
service provider of Thailand, contributed milestone data for flights to and from Thai airports, covering
connections with Singapore and Japan as well as Thai domestic flights, for June to
September 2025. The data were provided in the PBWG milestone format used in this note: off-block,
take-off, range-ring crossings at 40 and 100 NM, landing and in-block, each with time and, for the
ring crossings, position and altitude. They could therefore be used without conversion.

The contribution shows what partner data add to the approach. The European sample observes flights
from the European side; the Thai data observe the other end of the flight, at Bangkok Suvarnabhumi
(VTBS) and Don Mueang (VTBD), with the same milestones and definitions (@tbl-tha-overview). The ring
crossings lie on the 40 and 100 NM radii to within a fraction of a nautical mile, so they can be used
directly as contract points.

```{r tbl-tha-overview}
#| label: tbl-tha-overview
#| tbl-cap: "Milestone data contributed by AEROTHAI, 1 June – 30 September 2025. Shares refer to the Thai
#|   end of the flight."
#| eval: !expr has_ops && has_tha
tab_tha_overview(th) |> rename(Flow = FLOW) |> gt_tn()
```

For the international flows, the data describe the Thai part of each flight: the departure from
Thailand from off-block to the 100 NM ring, and the arrival in Thailand from the 100 NM ring to
in-block. @tbl-tha-segments summarises the duration of each segment. These durations are the building
blocks for the time offsets of this note: once a reference time is available for the same milestones,
for example from the filed plan, each segment yields a time offset in the same way as the European
range rings.

```{r tbl-tha-segments}
#| label: tbl-tha-segments
#| tbl-cap: "Duration of the departure and arrival segments at the Thai end of the flight (minutes, 15th
#|   percentile, median, 85th percentile), June – September 2025."
#| eval: !expr has_ops && has_tha
tab_tha_segments(th) |> gt_tn(groupname_col = "FLOW")
```

Two observations illustrate what the data can show. First, the segment from the 100 NM ring to the
40 NM ring is short and stable for both flows (median about 9–10 minutes). Second, the segment from the
40 NM ring to landing is longer for arrivals from Singapore (median 19.5 minutes) than from Japan
(15 minutes) (@fig-tha-arrival). The figure also shows a difference between the two Bangkok airports for
arrivals from Japan: at Don Mueang most flights land about 11 minutes after the 40 NM ring, while at
Suvarnabhumi the distribution is wider. This is the terminal part of the arrival, where sequencing takes
place. Differences between flows and aerodromes are a first indication of where arrival management
absorbs time, and of where a time constraint agreed in a TBO environment would need to be delivered.

```{r fig-tha-arrival}
#| label: fig-tha-arrival
#| fig-cap: "Arrivals in Thailand: duration of the 100–40 NM segment and of the 40 NM-to-landing
#|   segment, by flow and arrival aerodrome. Data contributed by AEROTHAI."
#| fig-height: 4
#| eval: !expr has_ops && has_tha
plot_tha_arrival(th)
```

**Example: SIA720, Singapore–Bangkok (A350).** A typical arrival: the aircraft crossed the 100 NM ring,
reached the 40 NM ring about 9 minutes later, landed about 20 minutes after that and was in-block about
9 minutes after landing. Each of these times is an observed contract point at the Thai end. Combined
with a reference trajectory for the same flight, they give the arrival-side time offsets that the
European record cannot observe.

The contributed period does not overlap with flights between Europe and Thailand in this note's
international sample, so the data are not yet joined to the European records. The structure is
nevertheless identical. The same contribution for flights to and from Europe would close the gap at
Bangkok shown in @tbl-intl-sources, where many departures to Europe are currently not observed from
European sources.

### What the international examples show

- The method transfers unchanged: the same milestones, the same contract table and the same measures.
- The **binding constraint is observation**, not method. The filed plan defines the milestones
  globally; observed actual times exist only where a region, or an open source, records them.
- The **observation status** makes the gap explicit and countable. Each partner contribution, such as
  ring crossings, FIR entries, landing and in-block times, closes a measurable part of it.

## Conclusions and next steps {#sec-conclusions}

This note set out to explore how trajectory-based operations can be measured from an operational
performance perspective, and to test a practical approach on synthetic and real data.

1. **Contract delivery, not deviation.** Measures are anchored on a declared reference trajectory, keep
   their sign, and are reported separately for time, lateral and vertical dimensions. Adherence and
   efficiency are not mixed.
2. **The reference must be declared.** For regulated flights, delivery against the filed plan and
   against the regulated plan tell different stories. Both are needed, and the revision–execution split
   connects them exactly in time.
3. **Milestones scale; continuous measures explain.** Range rings, top of climb and descent, and FIR
   crossings provide a compact, comparable view that works with sparse data. Continuous cross-track and
   along-track measures explain what happened between milestones where dense data exist.
4. **Observation status is part of the measure.** Extrapolated or proxy values are labelled and kept
   out of delivery statistics, so that missing observations are visible rather than hidden.
5. **Partners can close the gaps directly.** Milestone times at the partner end (ring crossings, FIR
   entries, landing and in-block) are sufficient to extend the European demonstration to full
   origin–destination coverage. The contribution from AEROTHAI (@sec-tha) shows that the format works
   as intended: the data could be used without conversion and describe the arrival and departure
   segments at the partner end with the same milestones.

Proposed next steps for the PBWG:

- agree a minimal **measurement specification**: reference versions and cut-off times, milestone set,
  ring radii, tolerances and aggregation rules;
- invite partners to contribute **milestone observations** for the study airports in the common
  table format;
- extend the European demonstration to a **season**;
- explore **predictability** and **revision history** as data on archived predictions and agreement
  versions become available.

## Appendix A – Data used and observation status {#sec-annex-data .appendix}

This appendix describes the data used in this note by **role**, so that partners can map them to
their own data holdings. How the European data were extracted is documented separately for internal
use; it depends on systems that are specific to EUROCONTROL and is not required to apply the method.
It is available as a companion report in the project repository (`TN-03-internal-processing.qmd`).

| Role | Content | European demonstration | Partner equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference trajectory | Filed flight plan as a 4D profile (position, time, level) | Network Manager trajectory based on the last filed plan (Model 1) | Filed plan processed by the regional flight data processing system |
| Revised reference | Plan updated after a flow management measure | Network Manager regulated trajectory (Model 2) | Revised plan or slot-adjusted plan, where recorded |
| Actual trajectory | Flown trajectory with time and level | Network Manager flown trajectory (Model 3), based on surveillance | Surveillance-based track (radar, ADS-B) |
| Observed milestones | Times of ring crossings, take-off, landing, off- and in-block | Derived from the actual trajectory; airport data (TN-01, TN-02) | Airport and ANSP records in the PBWG milestone format |
| Open observations | Ring crossings near partner airports | OpenSky Network | — |
| Partner contribution | Milestones at the partner end of the flight | AEROTHAI, Thailand (June–September 2025) | Any partner, same format |

: Data used by role. {#tbl-annex-roles}

| Sample | Period | Flights | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| European city pairs (6 directions) | 1–14 June 2025 | 950, of which 611 regulated | @sec-eur, @sec-rp4-tests |
| Reroute sample (10 European study airports) | 1–14 June 2025 | about 2,000 candidates; 100 examined | @sec-eur |
| International connections (7 partner airports) | 1–7 June 2025 | 1,532 | @sec-intl |
| AEROTHAI contribution | 1 June – 30 September 2025 | about 35,000 | @sec-tha |

: Samples. {#tbl-annex-samples}

**Observation status.** Every actual milestone carries one of four values:

| Status | Meaning | Used in measures |
|---|---|---|
| observed | Value derived from a surveillance report or a recorded event (including partner and open data) | yes |
| proxy | Value derived by a stated rule from other observed data | yes, labelled |
| extrapolated | Value copied or shifted from the reference, e.g. outside a region's surveillance area | no ("not observed") |
| missing | No value | no |

: Observation status. {#tbl-annex-status}

**Source order at the partner end.** Where several sources provide a milestone, the first available is
used: partner data, open surveillance data (ring crossings), regional surveillance positions with points
on both sides of the ring within five minutes, and finally the regional flown trajectory if it differs
from the plan.

**Times** are in UTC throughout.
